problem: Multimodal fine-tuning can exceed client compute budgets even when only a small part of the model is trainable.
contribution: MPSL keeps modality tokenizers on clients and trains a shared server encoder through aggregated local losses and returned cut-layer gradients.
reading_guide: Separate client compute savings from task accuracy, and distinguish raw retrieval recall from scores normalized to centralized training.

diagram.title: Tokenize locally, train jointly
diagram.description: Clients send modality tokens to a shared server encoder and prediction head. Predictions return to clients, which compute loss with local labels. The server aggregates these losses for one backward pass, then returns cut-layer gradients to update the local tokenizers.

stages.title: Modality tokenizers
stages.detail: Convert local image, audio or text inputs into tokens.

stages.title: Shared encoder
stages.detail: Encode tokens and return predictions through the task head.

stages.title: Local loss
stages.detail: Use private labels to calculate each client loss.

stages.title: Shared backward pass
stages.detail: Aggregate client losses and send cut-layer gradients back to the tokenizers.

diagram.footnote: Cut-layer gradients close the loop. Early fusion concatenates tokens before encoding; late fusion encodes modalities separately before combining them. No client-model weight averaging is required during training.

results.title: Compute savings with task-dependent accuracy
results.question: Does reducing client computation preserve classification accuracy on every task?
results.context: Meta-Transformer ViT-B/16; 100 clients with Dirichlet α=0.1. Selected classification tasks, accuracy (%) with reported ± terms over three seeds; higher is better. Client GFLOPs per input are lower-is-better.
results.interpretation: MPSL sharply lowers client compute and improves MELD over FedAvg, but trails FedAvg by 7.3 points on COCO-QA and 4.4 on Kinetics-Sounds.
results.caveat: These tasks expose both gains and deficits; they are three of five classification datasets. GFLOPs measure client work, not total system work or latency. The paper does not specify the type of ± interval.

results.title: Retrieval improves over distributed baselines
results.question: Does MPSL close the gap to centralized image-text retrieval?
results.context: Image-to-text retrieval, 100 clients; top-1 recall (%) with reported ± terms over three seeds, higher is better. Full ViT-B/16 encoder fine-tuning; raw recall, not normalized scores.
results.interpretation: MPSL improves on both evaluated distributed alternatives but remains well below centralized recall on both datasets.
results.caveat: The table also reports text-to-image retrieval and R@10; the selected rows isolate one direction and recall threshold. The reported ± convention is unspecified.

results.title: Retrieval depends on batch size
results.question: How sensitive is distributed retrieval to the available batch size?
results.context: MPSL with 25 clients. Top-1 retrieval recall normalized to centralized fine-tuning (% of reference performance); higher is better. These values are ratios, not raw recall.
results.interpretation: Larger batches substantially improve normalized recall over batch size 50, although the Flickr30K trend is not monotonic.
results.caveat: No uncertainty is tabulated. Larger retrieval batches are marked infeasible because of dataset partition sizes; this ablation uses fewer clients than the raw-recall table.

evaluation.label: Data
evaluation.value: COCO-QA, T4SA, Kinetics-Sounds, UCF101, MELD, MS-COCO and Flickr30K; image/text, image/audio and audio/text pairs.

evaluation.label: Models
evaluation.value: Meta-Transformer ViT-B/16; encoder-size analysis spans ViT-Tiny to ViT-Huge. Classification typically tunes the last six blocks; retrieval tunes the complete encoder.

evaluation.label: Compared with
evaluation.value: Centralized fine-tuning, FedAvg and FedCLIP; 25 or 100 clients with non-IID class partitions.

evaluation.label: Evaluation model
evaluation.value: Client tokenizers are aggregated after training and combined with the shared server model for comparison with federated baselines.

limitations: Accuracy is task-dependent: client compute savings do not imply matching FedAvg or centralized performance on every benchmark.
Retrieval needs sufficiently large batches; limited client data can make larger batch settings infeasible.
Missing modalities, client dropouts and heterogeneous edge hardware are explicitly left for future work.
Keeping raw labels local does not itself establish a formal privacy guarantee, and reported client GFLOPs do not establish end-to-end speed or energy gains.
takeaways: Offloading a frozen or trainable encoder can save client computation that parameter-efficient federated tuning still requires locally.
Batch size and fusion strategy matter: neither distributed retrieval nor multimodal fusion has one universally best setting.
